n: The groom praises his bride from her feet upward, calling her a prince’s daughter — noble in bearing. Her graceful form is like jewelry crafted by a master artist.

f.g: A noble woman — a title of honor, not necessarily literal royalty.

n: In the bold imagery of ancient love poetry, he compares her body to a full goblet and a heap of wheat bordered with lilies — signs of abundance and fruitfulness.

f.g: A sign of plenty at harvest.

n: He repeats an earlier image of gentle twin gazelles.
Her neck is graceful like an ivory tower, her eyes deep and clear like the pools of Heshbon, and her profile noble like a watchtower facing Damascus.

f.g: A city east of the Jordan, known for its reservoirs.
“Daughter of many” — probably a gate of Heshbon.

n: Her head is majestic like Mount Carmel, and her hair shines with a royal sheen. The king is captivated by her tresses.

f.g: A beautiful, wooded mountain on Israel’s coast.
Better “tresses” — the king is held captive by her locks.

n: He exclaims how beautiful and delightful she is, his love.
She is tall and graceful like a palm tree, a symbol of beauty and uprightness.

f.g: Tamar in Hebrew, also used as a woman’s name.

n: He longs to draw close to her, delighting in her fragrance and beauty.
Her kisses are like the finest wine, flowing smoothly. The bride finishes his sentence, saying the wine is “for my beloved.”
The bride affirms that she belongs to her beloved and that his desire is for her. This reverses the sad note of Genesis 3:16, showing love restored to harmony.

f.r: Genesis 3:16; Song of Solomon 2:16; Song of Solomon 6:3

n: She invites him to go out with her into the countryside and spend the night in the villages.
Let’s rise early, she says, to see whether the vines and pomegranates are blooming. There she will give him her love.
The mandrakes give off their scent, and she has saved every kind of delicious fruit, new and old, for him.

f.g: A plant thought in ancient times to promote love and fertility (Genesis 30:14-16).
